title: At the bazaar: prices, bargaining, and big numbers
goal: Ask prices, bargain in the right tone, and read numbers up to a hundred — the part of Urdu that takes the most memorizing.
bekal: ask prices with کتنے کا / کتنے کی
recognize the patterns in the numbers 20–100 and the units لاکھ and کروڑ

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — انارکلی بازار
dialogs.intro: Anarkali Bazaar, late afternoon. Budi stops at a cloth stall, holding up a shirt.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: بھائی صاحب، یہ قمیض کتنے کی ہے؟
lines.baca: bhāī sāhab, ye qamīz kitne kī hai?
lines.id: Brother, how much is this shirt?
lines.literal: brother sir, this shirt how-many of-(f) is?

lines.speaker: دکاندار:
lines.text: دو ہزار روپے، صاحب۔ بہت اچھا کپڑا ہے۔
lines.baca: do hazār rūpaye, sāhab. bahut achchhā kapṛā hai.
lines.id: Two thousand rupees, sir. It's very good cloth.
lines.literal: two thousand rupees, sir. very good cloth is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: Two thousand? That's a bit much.

lines.speaker: دکاندار:
lines.text: نہیں صاحب، یہ بہت کم ہے۔ اٹھارہ سو۔
lines.baca: nahīñ sāhab, ye bahut kam hai. aṭhārah sau.
lines.id: No, sir, that's far too little. Eighteen hundred.
lines.literal: no sir, this very little is. eighteen hundred.

lines.speaker: دکاندار:
lines.text: چلیں، آپ کے لیے پندرہ سو۔ کون سا رنگ؟
lines.baca: chaleñ, āp ke liye pandrah sau. kaun sā rañg?
lines.id: All right, for you fifteen hundred. Which color?
lines.literal: come-on, you of for fifteen hundred. which color?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: Blue. Do you have my size?

lines.speaker: دکاندار:
lines.text: جی، سب سائز ہیں۔ اور کچھ؟
lines.baca: jī, sab sāiz haiñ. aur kuchh?
lines.literal: yes, all sizes are. and something?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: No, that's all. Here's the money.

lines.speaker: دکاندار:
lines.id: Thank you, sir. Please come again.

notes: **Prices are asked with کتنے کا or کتنے کی, depending on the item.** The word قمیض is feminine, so کتنے کی. The word کرتا (a long men's tunic) is masculine, so کتنے کا. If you forget the gender, there's a safe route that's always right: **قیمت کیا ہے؟** ("what's the price?") — قیمت is always feminine and the sentence never changes.

**Hundreds are counted in a surprising way — or not, for English speakers.** "One thousand five hundred" isn't ایک ہزار پانچ سو but **پندرہ سو** — "fifteen hundred". This pattern is used for every number between 1,100 and 1,900, just like English *fifteen hundred*. At the bazaar, almost all haggling happens in سو.

**Bargaining is expected, but keep the tone light.** The right opening isn't "too expensive" but **تھوڑا زیادہ ہے** ("it's a bit much") or **تھوڑا کم کیجیے** ("bring it down a little"). A blunt refusal — یہ بہت مہنگا ہے — sounds like you're accusing the seller of cheating. Once the price is right: ٹھیک ہے.

**The word بس is one of the most useful words in all of Urdu.** It means "enough", "that's it", "stop". The question بس؟ = "is that all?". The exclamation بس! = "enough!". The phrase بس اتنا ہی = "just that much". At a café, when someone is pouring your tea, بس بس stops them politely.

**You'll hear تشریف لائیے often, and it's worth recognizing.** Literally "bring your honor" — a very polite way of saying "please come" or "please come in". Its cousin: تشریف رکھیے ("please have a seat"). You don't need to use it yet, but recognizing it unlocks Urdu courtesy much faster.

**The words کچھ and کوئی split the work.** The word کچھ is for things and amounts: اور کچھ؟ ("anything else?"), کچھ پانی ("some water"). The word کوئی is for people and countable units: کوئی اور؟ ("anyone else?"), کوئی مسئلہ نہیں ("no problem").

grammars.title: The pattern of numbers 20 to 100
body: Urdu has a hundred number words that each stand on their own, and there's no point pretending they're guessable. But two patterns help your ear catch them much faster than your eye, and they're worth knowing from the start.

**Pattern one: the tens ending stays the same.** All the 20s end in ـیس, the 30s in ـتیس, the 40s in ـالیس, the 50s in ـاون, the 60s in ـسٹھ, the 70s in ـہتر, the 80s in ـاسی, the 90s in ـانوے. As soon as you hear the ending, you know the tens.
after: **Pattern two: numbers ending in 9 are built as "one less".** The prefix اُن- means "one less than", so انتیس (29) literally means "one less than thirty". The same pattern gives انیس (19), انتالیس (39), انچاس (49), انسٹھ (59), انہتر (69), اناسی (79), نناوے (99).
The full list 1–100 is at the back of the book. Don't learn it all at once — learn what you need: prices, ages, house numbers, and years.

grammars.title: Money and big units
body: Pakistan's currency is the روپیہ (*rūpayā*), the word that gave English "rupee". Its plural is روپے (*rūpaye*), and the plural is always used with numbers.
after: ⚠️ Urdu **doesn't count in millions**. One million is دس لاکھ ("ten lakh"), and a hundred million is دس کروڑ. If you read Pakistani or Indian news, every economic figure appears in these two units — and your brain needs time to stop converting them into millions. You'll also see them written 10,00,000 with lakh-style commas.

blocks.title: Six sentences that cover the whole transaction
items: Opening: یہ کتنے کا ہے؟ or قیمت کیا ہے؟ — "how much is it?"
Bargaining: تھوڑا کم کیجیے۔ ("bring it down a little") · آخری قیمت کیا ہے؟ ("what's your final price?")
Declining politely: نہیں، شکریہ۔ میں بعد میں آتا ہوں۔ ("no thanks, I'll come back later") — and this often brings the price down.
Closing: ٹھیک ہے، دے دیجیے۔ ("OK, I'll take it") · یہ لیجیے۔ ("here you are") · باقی پیسے؟ ("my change?")

exercises.prompt: Write these numbers as Urdu words.
Choose کتنے کا or کتنے کی.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: پچیس — چالیس — سڑسٹھ — ننانوے — ڈیڑھ سو
کتنے کی — کتنے کا — کتنے کی — کتنے کے — کتنے کی
قیمت کیا ہے؟ — تھوڑا زیادہ ہے۔ — تھوڑا کم کیجیے۔ — ٹھیک ہے، میں لیتا ہوں۔ — اور کچھ؟ نہیں، بس۔
یہ قمیض کتنے کی ہے؟ — یہ تھوڑا زیادہ ہے۔ — تھوڑا کم کیجیے۔ — آخری قیمت کیا ہے؟ — پندرہ سو روپے ہیں۔
wave: Learn 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, and 90 today — just eight words. The rest stick on their own once the tens are in place.
